questions.question: Give the Gram stain, catalase (if relevant), and confirmatory test for Streptococcus agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, Candida albicans, and Enterococcus.
questions.question_raw:
Q66 (2013 AM, 2015)
What is the gram, catalase (if relevant), confirmatory test for: Strep agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, Candida albicans, Enterococcus

parts.text: Give the Gram stain, catalase, and confirmatory test for each organism.

parts_raw.text: Give gram stain, catalase, and confirmatory test for each organism

questions.model_answer:
Streptococcus agalactiae: gram-positive cocci, catalase negative, Lancefield group B antigen (also CAMP/hippurate positive).
Proteus vulgaris: gram-negative bacilli, catalase positive, oxidase negative, swarming/urease positive, indole positive (distinguishes from P. mirabilis).
Candida albicans: gram-positive yeast, germ-tube positive (and chlamydospore formation).
Enterococcus: gram-positive cocci in pairs/short chains, catalase negative, PYR positive with bile-esculin hydrolysis and growth in 6.5% NaCl; reacts with Lancefield group D antisera.
questions.beyond_mandell: Identification data for S. agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, and Candida albicans are from standard clinical microbiology (Murray Manual of Clinical Microbiology); this chapter covers only the Enterococcus tests.

cohort_answer.text:
GPC, cat neg, Lancefield antigen test
GNB, cat pos, índole pos, ornithine decarboxylase neg (mirabilis - pos)
Gram pos, cat pos, germ tube positive (dublinensis is the only other pos germ tube)
GPC, weakly pos/ usually cat neg, bile eschulin hydrolysis (grows well in 6.5% NaCl)

questions.question: Practical station: laboratory isolate - gram-positive cocci in chains, beta-hemolytic on blood agar plate, CAMP test positive, hippurate hydrolysis positive. Name the organism.
questions.question_raw: Practical station: BacT (Powerpoint) isolate - GPB, beta-hemolytic on BAP, CAMP positive, hippurate positive.
questions.model_answer: a) Streptococcus agalactiae (Lancefield group B streptococcus). The combination of a beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive coccus in chains that is CAMP-positive and hippurate-hydrolysis-positive is characteristic of S. agalactiae.
questions.beyond_mandell: Identifying biochemistry (CAMP and hippurate positivity) is standard clinical microbiology (Mandell Ch. 201 identifies the organism but does not detail these tests in the slice read).

questions.question: Give the Gram stain, colony morphology, catalase (if applicable) and rapid bench identification test and result for the following organisms.
questions.question_raw: 21. Give Gram stain, colony morphology, catalase (if applicable) and rapid bench ID test and result for: a) Group B Strep; b) Enterococcus spp.; c) Candida albicans; d) Proteus vulgaris
questions.model_answer:
a) Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae): Gram-positive cocci in chains; grey-white colonies with a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood agar; catalase negative; rapid test - Lancefield group B latex agglutination positive (CAMP test positive, hippurate hydrolysis positive; bacitracin resistant).
b) Enterococcus species: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains; small grey non-haemolytic (alpha or gamma) colonies; catalase negative (may be weakly/pseudo-positive); rapid test - PYR positive and bile-esculin positive with growth in 6.5% NaCl (LAP positive).
c) Candida albicans: budding yeast, stains Gram-positive; white creamy pasty colonies, may show 'feet' (marginal hyphal fringe) on cornmeal/agar; catalase not applicable; rapid test - germ tube positive in serum at 3 h (also C. dubliniensis), with terminal chlamydospores and pseudohyphae on cornmeal-Tween 80.
d) Proteus vulgaris: Gram-negative bacilli; swarming waves of growth over blood agar, lactose non-fermenter, produces H2S; catalase positive, oxidase negative; rapid test - urease positive (rapid) and indole positive (distinguishing it from indole-negative P. mirabilis); ornithine decarboxylase negative (positive in P. mirabilis).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort called Enterococcus 'catalase weak positive'; enterococci are catalase negative (a weak pseudocatalase reaction may be seen on blood-containing media).

cohort_answer.text:
GBS – GPC chains, catalase negative, beta hemolytic, lancefield group B
Enterococcus – GPC pairs/chains, catalase weak positive, alpha or gamma hemolytic, PYR + (GAS too), LAP, bile esculin positive
Candida albicans – "Gram positive" yeast, feet on morphology, germ tube + (also dublinesis), pseudohyphae on wet mount (also with glabrata)
Proteus vulgaris – GNB, catalase +, swarming colony, indole positive, OTC neg (mirabilis +), urease +

questions.question: Group B streptococcal intrapartum prophylaxis: indications and antibiotics of choice.
questions.question_raw:
Q18 (2004 PM)
Group B Strep ppx

parts_raw.text: A) Indications and abx of choice

questions.model_answer: a) Screen all pregnant women with vaginal-rectal culture at 35-37 weeks. Indications for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP): (1) previous infant with invasive GBS disease; (2) GBS bacteriuria during any trimester of the current pregnancy; (3) positive GBS vaginal-rectal screening culture in current pregnancy; (4) unknown GBS status at onset of labor plus any of - delivery <37 weeks, membrane rupture >=18 h, intrapartum temperature >=38.0 C (100.4 F), or intrapartum NAAT positive for GBS. Not indicated if planned cesarean before labor with intact membranes, or negative screen in current pregnancy. Antibiotics: Penicillin G is the drug of choice - 5 million units IV initially, then 2.5-3.0 million units every 4 h until delivery. Ampicillin 2 g IV then 1 g every 4 h is an acceptable alternative. For penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis risk: cefazolin 2 g then 1 g every 8 h. For high anaphylaxis risk: clindamycin 900 mg every 8 h only if isolate confirmed susceptible (including negative inducible resistance), otherwise vancomycin 1 g every 12 h until delivery.

cohort_answer.text: Screen all women for colonization at week 35-37 weeks gestation (vaginal + rectal swab). Indications for ppx: if screen +, previous infant with invasive GBS, GBS bacteriuria during any trimester of current pregnancy or GBS status unknown at onset of labor if <37 weeks (if unknown status and >37 weeks, give if membranes ruptured >18h). PPx: PenG 5 mU then 2.5-3mU q4h until delivery. Alternative: Ampicillin 2g IV or Cefazolin 2g IV at least 4h before birth

questions.question: State the preferred treatments for the following.
questions.question_raw: Preferred treatments: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy; Group B strep ppx
questions.model_answer:
a) Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (CDC-recommended in pregnancy); alternatives are amoxicillin 500 mg PO tid x7 days or erythromycin, with a test of cure at 3-4 weeks. Doxycycline and fluoroquinolones are contraindicated.
b) Intrapartum penicillin G 5 million units IV then 2.5-3 million units q4h (or ampicillin 2 g IV then 1 g q4h) given at least 4 h before delivery; cefazolin 2 g IV then 1 g q8h for low-risk penicillin allergy. Screen at 35-37 weeks gestation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Group B streptococcus intrapartum prophylaxis is not covered in this Chlamydia chapter; part b rests on CDC/ACOG GBS prevention guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy: Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. Group B strep ppx: IV PenG 5mU or Ampicillin 2g IV or Cefazolin 2g IV at least 4h before birth. Risk factors for neonatal GBS sepsis: maternal colonization during current pregnancy, GBS bacteriuria, prior infant with invasive GBS disease, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever. For colonization, risk of sepsis is 1-2%. Screen women at 35-37 weeks GA.

questions.question: Series of scenarios with varying gestational age, presence or absence of maternal fever, duration of premature rupture of membranes, cesarean or vaginal delivery, and penicillin allergy status. Would you give prophylaxis, and if so with what antibiotic?
questions.question_raw: Series of scenarios with different gestational ages, fever or not, duration of PROM, C/S or not, PCN allergy or not.

parts.text: Would you give prophylaxis, and if so with what antibiotic?

parts_raw.text: Would you give ppx and if so, with what abx?

questions.model_answer: a) Give intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis when any of the following is present: previous infant with invasive GBS, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, positive GBS screen this pregnancy, or unknown status at labor with delivery <37 weeks, membrane rupture >=18 h, or intrapartum temperature >=38.0 C. Do NOT give if a negative screen this pregnancy, or planned cesarean before labor onset with intact membranes (regardless of colonization). If maternal chorioamnionitis/fever with suspected amnionitis is present, replace GBS prophylaxis with broad-spectrum therapy that includes an agent active against GBS. Antibiotic: penicillin G 5 million units then 2.5-3.0 million units every 4 h until delivery (first choice); ampicillin as alternative. Penicillin-allergic, low anaphylaxis risk: cefazolin 2 g then 1 g every 8 h. High anaphylaxis risk: clindamycin 900 mg every 8 h only if susceptibility (with inducible resistance testing) confirmed, otherwise vancomycin 1 g every 12 h until delivery.
questions.beyond_mandell: Neonatal management arms of the cohort answer (in-hospital observation periods, whether a well vs unwell infant gets a septic workup) follow CDC/AAP and CPS neonatal algorithms; Mandell (p. 2511) supports full evaluation plus empirical treatment for infants with sepsis signs and observation >=48 h for preterm or ROM >=18 h without adequate IAP.

cohort_answer.text: If infant unwell, do full septic work-up and treat - classically ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. If infant well, treatment/prophylaxis depends on risk factors. If mother GBS positive with adequate IAP, no treatment needed. If GBS positive and inadequate IAP, CPS recommends close physical assessment and in-hospital observation at least 24 hours, reassess between 24-48 hours (or keep 48h if parents not trusted); no prophylaxis indicated. If maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes AND GBS positive, regardless of IAP, close physical exam and observation up to 48 hours warranted, no antimicrobial prophylaxis. If mother has chorioamnionitis she should get broad IAP; debate whether infant should get antibiotics or just be closely observed (CDC/AAP favor former, CPS no firm position); if no IAP given for maternal chorioamnionitis then neonate should likely get ongoing therapy.
